```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
```

The more digested a prey item, the coarser the rank it can be named to. That
matters because digestion is not even across prey. Soft-bodied prey lose their
identifying features faster than fish with otoliths or crustaceans with hard
parts, so the material that can still be identified to species is a biased
sample of what was eaten. Buckland et al. (2017) asked diet studies to report
how prey condition affected identification. `dv_digestion_diagnostic()` gives
you that table.

```{r setup}
library(DietView)
dat <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "dietview_example.csv", package = "DietView"),
                na.strings = c("NA", ""))
lin <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "dietview_example_lineage.csv", package = "DietView"),
                na.strings = c("NA", ""))
spec <- dv_spec(predator = "predator_species_common_name", stomach = "stomach_id",
                prey_id = "aphia_id", prey_name = "verified_name",
                weight = "prey_weight", digestion = "digestion_level_id",
                covariates = "period")
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = lin, verbose = FALSE)
```

## What the diagnostic computes

For every record, DietView finds the deepest rank with a name: its *finest
resolved rank*. Records with no name at any rank are "Unresolved". Within each
digestion score it then reports the share of records, and of weight, at each
finest rank.

```{r diag}
diag <- dv_digestion_diagnostic(prep)
out  <- diag[, c("digestion", "finest_rank", "n_records", "p_records", "p_weight")]
out[c("p_records", "p_weight")] <- round(out[c("p_records", "p_weight")], 1)
out
```

Percentages are computed within each digestion score, so each score adds up to
100% whatever its sample size. Always read them next to `n_records`. In this
invented example the scores hold
`r paste(tapply(diag$n_records, diag$digestion, sum), collapse = ", ")` records
respectively, far too few for any pattern to mean anything.

## Drawing it

```{r plot}
m <- xtabs(p_records ~ finest_rank + digestion, data = diag)
barplot(m, col = grDevices::hcl.colors(nrow(m), "Blues"), legend.text = TRUE,
        args.legend = list(x = "topright", cex = 0.7, bg = "white"),
        xlab = "Digestion score", ylab = "% of records")
```

## How to read it on real data

- If the species share falls steeply with digestion, fine-rank results rest
  mostly on fresh material. Consider reporting them for scores 1–2 separately,
  with the sample size you lose by doing so.
- Weight is affected twice: digested prey are both harder to name and lighter.
  A steep profile is a reason to be cautious with the weight currency in
  particular.
- Use `by =` to check whether the profile differs between strata, for example
  between periods, when observers or protocols changed between them.

```{r by}
by_period <- dv_digestion_diagnostic(prep, by = "period")
by_period[c("p_records", "p_weight")] <- round(by_period[c("p_records", "p_weight")], 1)
head(by_period, 8)
```

The diagnostic describes identification; it does not correct for it. The
vignette "A known diet" shows, on simulated data where the true diet is known,
how much a diet description moves when unidentified material is kept or dropped.

## Reference

Buckland, A., Baker, R., Loneragan, N., & Sheaves, M. (2017). Standardising fish
stomach content analysis: the importance of prey condition. *Fisheries Research*,
196, 126–140.
